section_title: What happens when the people put what they have learned into practice?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 13 On the second day of the month, the heads of all the families, along with the priests and Levites, gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law. 14 And they found written in the Law, which the LORD had commanded through Moses, that the Israelites were to dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month, 15 and that they should proclaim this message and spread it throughout their towns and in Jerusalem, saying, “Go out to the hill country and bring back branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees, to make booths, as it is written.”

16 And the people went out, brought back branches, and made booths on their own rooftops, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, and in the squares by the Water Gate and by the Gate of Ephraim. 17 The whole assembly that had returned from exile made booths and lived in them. From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this. And there was great rejoicing. 18 Day after day, from the first day to the last, Ezra read from the Book of the Law of God. The Israelites kept the feast for seven days, and on the eighth day they held an assembly, according to the ordinance.

context_lines: The following day, family heads, priests and Levites gather around Ezra to study further. They find the command to live in booths during the seventh-month feast and spread instructions to gather branches.

The people make these temporary shelters on rooftops, in courtyards, in the temple courts and in the public squares. [Leviticus 23:33–43](https://biblehub.com/bsb/leviticus/23.htm) explains their purpose: later generations are to remember that God made Israel dwell in booths when He brought them out of Egypt.

The whole returning assembly participates with great joy. Ezra reads from the Law each day through the seven-day feast, followed by the assembly on the eighth day. Learning leads to a shared act of remembrance and obedience.
common_interpretation_lines: [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/nehemiah/8.htm) understands the statement that Israel had not celebrated like this since Joshua as describing the celebration’s particular thoroughness and joy. He notes earlier observances, including [Ezra 3:4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ezra/3.htm). [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/nehemiah/8.htm) emphasizes putting the recovered instruction into practice and connects the temporary shelters with the life of God’s people as travelers who depend on Him.
god_plan_lines: The Feast of Tabernacles also appears in [Zechariah 14:9, 16–21](https://biblehub.com/bsb/zechariah/14.htm), where the Lord is King over all the earth and survivors from the nations come to worship Him and celebrate the feast.

This is a scriptural connection through the same feast. In Nehemiah, the returned community remembers God’s care on the journey from Egypt; Zechariah places the feast within a larger picture of the nations honoring the Lord as King. The worship described there reaches beyond the community gathered here.
